sent.t: Seven pieces.
I counted them last Tuesday, standing in front of my mother's tansu, and I had to sit down on the tatami.
Everything else in that closet is noise.
Not because I am thinner than you, I am one meter fifty-two, and I weigh what I weigh.
And not because I am richer, my white shirt costs less than four pizzas.
It is the cut, and it is one rule my mother used on every bride in Gion.
The piece has to hold your body up, not hang on it.
When it hangs, people see the hanger, and the hanger makes a woman look tired before she opens her mouth.
The last piece is the one nobody in America knows.
8 inches of silk from 1975, and on Friday it goes into Kero's suitcase.
My mother was Fumiko Arai.
She dressed brides and geiko in June for 40 years, and I grew up between the mirrors of her shop in Nishijin.
Then I lived 19 years in California, in Sunnyvale, because my husband Hiroshi was an engineer there, so I know your closet.
I know the mall, the sales, the three black jackets, the sweater you keep for a cold restaurant.
I did it the American way too.
Here is what I learned, and it took me 40 years.
A piece you own forever has to pass three questions.
Does it hold its shape after 20 washes, or does it go soft at the collar and lie down?
Does it work with the other six pieces or does it need a special friend?
Can you sit on the floor in it in a matchia in February and get up without holding the table?
That is the test nobody asks in a shop.
People tell me the answer is a bigger closet.
In Sunnyvale, I had a closet the size of this kitchen and I still stood in front of it every morning with nothing to wear.
The clothes were there, the system was not.
A closet with 40 pieces and no rules is just 40 decisions before breakfast.
And by the time you make them, your face is tired and you put on the black jacket again.
Seven pieces is not a punishment.
It is a rest.
It is the same reason a good kitchen has one good knife and not 11 bad ones.
And before we start, I want you to do something with me.
Go to a window with good daylight and take two things from your closet.
One black, one white, a shirt or a scarf, whatever you have.
Hold the black under your chin and look.
Then the white.
Do not look at the color.
Look at the line under your jaw, under your eyes.
With the black, that line gets deeper.
It is not your face.
It is the shadow.
This is the whole video in one minute and it costs nothing.
Yui did it on Sunday with my black cardigan and she said, Grandma, I look like I have not slept.
That is the shadow.
Number 1.
A white cotton shirt with a collar that stands.
Not a blouse with a soft collar that folds over and dies at the second wash.
A shirt with a proper stand, the kind a man wears, in your size.
I have four.
One of them is 22 years old and the collar is still standing, because it is cotton with a little weight, not the thin stuff from
the big store.
In 1975, my mother dressed a bride in Gion, whose mother wore a white collar under her kimono, and Fumiko said, look, the collar is doing
half the work of the face.
A white collar throws light up under the jaw.
A black one eats it.
In summer, I wear Mr.
Okada's linen from his store in Nishiki, the rest of the year, cotton.
Mine cost $38 at a shop near Sanzhou and a good one lasts 10 years, which is $4 a year.
Tonight, take your white shirt and your black sweater to the window, both under your chin, one after the other.
Then take a photo with your phone.
The phone does not lie and the mirror is very polite.
Number 2.
A thin cardigan in Marino wool, the color of oatmeal or dark navy, no buttons you have to fight.
Thin, two ply if the label says it.
In February, the inside of this house is 35 degrees and in August it is 95 with the humidity of a wet towel.
A thick sweater is not warm, it is heavy.
In 2023, I had two thick knits on and I could not lift my arms to hang the laundry on the second floor.
Hiroshi found me standing on the stairs like a scarecrow.
My mother said, warmth is in the layer, not in the weight.
Thin wool under a thin wool, that is warm, and you can still move.
The thick fleece one is the trap.
It is soft in the shop and it makes your shoulders into two round balls.
My merino was $60.
I have had it 8 winters and I wash it at 86 degrees in a net bag and dry it flat on a tenugi.
Tonight, put on your thickest knit and raise both arms over your head.
If your shoulders climb up to your ears, that piece is not doing you a favor.
Fold it for your daughter and keep the thin one.
Number 3 Navy trousers, straight, sitting at your real waist, not black.
Black looks hard in daylight.
It shows every piece of lint from the tatami, and it makes the shadow we talked about.
Navy is softer, and it goes with the white shirt and with the oatmeal cardigan, so it works with the other six.
In 2016, I bought a pair one size too big because the waistband pinched me in the shop.
and all the way home on Imadegawa-dori, I was pulling them up in front of Yui.
That is not the trousers' fault.
That is the waistband's fault.
After sixty, the waist is the part that changes, not the hip, so you buy for the waist and let a woman with a machine fix
the rest.
Mine cost and a seamstress near Kawaramachi took $18 to shorten them and take in the waste.
Tonight, sit down on a chair in your trousers for one full minute, then stand up.
If you have to pull them up when you stand, they are not yours yet.
Take them to a tailor or give them away.
Number four, a square scarf, 27 inches, cotton or silk, in a color that puts light in your face, not a blanket.
I see women in Kyoto with a scarf the size of a tablecloth, and by the third block, it is a bag they carry on one
shoulder.
A small square is enough, folded corner to corner, once around the neck, one knot.
In March, Carol sent me a photo from Sacramento in a mustard scarf, and she wrote, Michiko, why does my face look grey?
The mustard was the same value as her skin, so the two melted into one, and her face disappeared.
We found a soft color for her, and in the next photo, she looked awake.
You do not need a new color, you need the color next to the face to be lighter or darker than the face.
Mr.
Okada keeps cotton remnants in a box at Nishiki, and a square with a hem costs eight dollars.
Tonight, take three scarves to the window, one at a time, and photograph yourself.
Choose the one where your eyes come forward, not the one you love, the one where your eyes come forward.
Number five, flat leather shoes that a man can re-sew.
Mrs.
Kinoshita lives across the street.
She is 81.
She walks the philosopher's path every morning, 10,000 steps, and she has had the same leather shoes for 15 years.
Last spring, she bought rubber shoes for the rain, new and light, and she slipped near the Eikando temple and sat on the wet stone for
a while.
The next morning, she put the old leather back on.
The cobbler near Demachianagi resolves them for $25, and they come back like new.
Leather takes the shape of your foot, and your foot at 68 is not the foot you had at 50.
It has its own map now.
A stiff sole does not run that map.
Mine cost $120 and I have resold them twice.
Tonight, pick up your shoe and bend it where the toes meet the sole.
If it does not bend, if it is a board, it will not walk with you.
It will make you walk on your heels and that is what people here before they see you.
Number 6 A small bag that crosses your body and leaves both hands free.
Carol came with a bag the size of a small suitcase, and at Kawaramachi Station she could not find her glasses because both hands were holding
the bag.
Mrs.
Kinoshita carries a bag the size of a paper bag with one strap across her chest.
Keys, glasses, a tanugi, a little purse.
That is all.
A heavy bag pulls one shoulder down and then you walk crooked and then your whole body looks tired even when it is not.
Mine was $45 at a shop in the station and the strap is wide enough that it does not cut.
Tonight put your bag on the kitchen scale.
If it is over 2 pounds, take everything out and put back only what you used this week.
You will be surprised what you have been carrying since March.
Before the last one, two small things.
If you have been with me since the beginning of this closet, press the like button.
It helps Yui and me more than you know.
And subscribe because next week Carol comes and I will open her suitcase on the tatami.
And now the seventh piece.
In 1975, my mother dressed a bride in Gion in a kimono with an obi the color of a persimmon.
When the bride left, Fumiko cut eight inches from the end of the obi and put it in her drawer because she said a good silk
should not disappear with one wedding.
She died in 2009.
That winter, I found the silk, and I sewed it into a small pouch with my own hands, badly.
The stitches are not straight.
It holds my keys.
It has no label and no price, and it is the piece I would save from the house.
On Friday, it goes into Carol's suitcase, with a note from me, because she is coming in April, and she will need somewhere to put her
keys.
You can do this.
There is one piece of fabric in your house that belonged to someone.
A scarf, a sleeve, a tablecloth from your mother.
Take it to a tailor, $10, and ask for a small pouch with a zip.
That is the seventh piece, and it costs $10 and a memory.
Tonight, open the drawer where you keep the things you do not use and find it.
Put it where you see it every morning.
next to your keys and you will understand why I cried on Tuesday.
So, seven pieces.
A white shirt with a standing collar, a thin cardigan, navy trousers at your waist, a small square scarf, flat leather shoes, a small bag, and
a piece with a person inside it.
You do not need to buy anything tonight.
Open your closet, take out the black thing and hold the white one under your chin at the window.
That is the whole beginning.
My mother used to say, your clothes speak before you do, so be careful what they say.
She was right for 40 years in Jiyo, and she is right in my kitchen in Nishijin.
Tell me in the comments, if you could keep only seven pieces, which one would be the first one you save?
Yui reads them to me with my tea on Sunday.
And in the next one, Carol arrives in April with two suitcases, and I show you the four things I take out of them before she
unpacks.
She will not be happy.
She will thank me later.
